segments.say: Lesson 18. L L M Evaluation Fundamentals. Golden datasets, offline versus online evals, L L M-as-judge, pairwise comparison and regression gating.

Evaluation (evals) means testing an L L M app on a fixed set of examples and scoring its answers, so you know whether a prompt or model change made things better or worse. Here is an analogy. Unit tests for software you can't fully predict. You can't eyeball every answer, so you keep a "golden" exam and re-grade the app after every change.

Why does this matter? L L M outputs vary and prompt changes can silently break other cases. Interviewers strongly favour candidates who mention evals without being asked. A few key words. Golden dataset: Curated inputs (and ideal outputs) used for testing. Evaluator: Code or an L L M judge that scores an output. L L M-as-judge: Using an L L M with a rubric to grade answers. Offline versus online eval: Before deploy versus on live traffic. Regression: Something that used to work now fails.

segments.say: The fix: a fixed test set scored automatically after every change. Ship v3, reject v2. That's an eval.
The eval-driven development loop. Start with a golden dataset: 50–200 representative inputs (with expected answers where possible), including edge cases and past failures.
Run the app version under test over every example.
Evaluators score each output: deterministic code checks (valid jason? contains citation?), L L M-as-judge (correct? helpful? faithful?) and sampled human review.
Aggregate metrics per version, and compare with the previous version side by side.
Regression gate in C I: block the prompt or model change if key metrics drop.
Ship it. L L M apps change behaviour with every prompt tweak, so evals are your unit tests.
Online evals on production traces (sampling plus judges plus thumbs up/down). New failures go back into the dataset, closing the loop.

Kinds of evaluators. Deterministic / heuristic: exact match, regex, jason schema validity, contains-citation, length, latency, cost. Reference-based: compare with the expected answer (semantic similarity, an L L M judging "same meaning?"). Reference-free L L M-as-judge: score against a rubric (helpfulness, tone, safety) without ground truth. Pairwise: the judge picks the better of A versus B. More reliable than absolute scores. Human: expert annotation queues, the gold standard for calibrating judges.

L L M-as-judge done right. Clear rubric, binary or small scales (pass/fail, 1–3) rather than 1–10. Ask for reasoning before the score. Calibrate against human labels and measure agreement. Watch the biases: position bias (swap A/B order), verbosity bias, self-preference for the same model family.

Agent-specific evals. Final response: did it solve the task. Trajectory: right tools, right order, no wasted steps. Single step: given this state, did it pick the right tool and arguments. Plus cost, latency and number of steps per task.
Gotchas. "Vibe checks" on 5 examples. Use a real dataset. Overfitting prompts to the eval set. Keep a held-out set. Only measuring accuracy. Also track latency, cost and safety.

Say it in the interview. "I treat evals as unit tests: a versioned golden dataset built from real queries and past failures, deterministic checks plus calibrated L L M-as-judge rubrics, pairwise comparisons between versions, and a C I gate so no prompt or model change ships if it regresses. In production I run online evals on sampled traces and feed failures back into the dataset.".

Let's compare. Exact / regex / schema: sometimes, about free, format, extraction, classification. Embedding similarity: yes, cheap, paraphrase-tolerant correctness. L L M-as-judge (rubric): optional, $ per eval, helpfulness, faithfulness, tone. Pairwise judge: no, $$, choosing between versions. Human review: optional, $$$, calibration, high stakes.

Offline versus online. When: before deploy (C I), on live traffic. Data: curated dataset, real traces. Ground truth: often available, rarely, so reference-free. Goal: prevent regressions, detect drift, find new failures.

A likely interview question: How do you evaluate an L L M app? A strong answer: Golden dataset from real cases, layered evaluators (code checks, L L M-as-judge with rubrics, humans for calibration), version comparison, a C I regression gate, and online evals on sampled production traces with a feedback loop.
That's it for L L M Evaluation Fundamentals. Now play the quiz and games in the app to lock it in. See you in the next lesson.
